utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Would the Registry, please, have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Prosecution, you have the floor. We have a relatively short week ahead of us. I believe we are going to be sitting today, this afternoon, tomorrow, Tuesday afternoon and Wednesday. How is that going to happen, then? What is happening on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are also scheduled to sit in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. So we are not sitting in the morning, Wednesday morning?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we have the three afternoons, Mr. Prosecutor. It is up to you, then, to do what you can so that things are arranged as best as possible. The other witness had to leave so the cross-examination will have to take place at a later date for that witness. Mr. Prosecutor, please introduce your next case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours and counsel. My next witness, Mr. President and your Honours, is Deborah Christie. Deborah Christie is an executive from the BBC. In 1993 she was a journalist and a film-maker employed by Granada Films in the United Kingdom. They made a film in 1993 entitled "We Are All Neighbours". It is a film about the village of Visnjica, one of the villages which is listed in the indictment and one of the villages which was attacked by the HVO in the Kiseljak municipality in April of 1993. Your Honours have already heard two witnesses who have testified about this attack; those are Witnesses AA and Witness CC. Ms Christie and her film crew were in Visnjica and in Kiseljak from 22nd January 1993 until 14th February of that same year. Following the attack on the village of Visnjica, she and her crew returned to Kiseljak and to the village on 29th April for additional film-making. She remained in Kiseljak and in Visnjica until 3rd May 1993. Her testimony will relate to her observations in and around Visnjica and Kiseljak before and after the attack by the HVO. She will describe the village of Visnjica, what it was like; what life was like in the village before and after the attack. She will also testify about events that occurred on the night of 4th February in Kiseljak. That specifically relates to the destruction of Muslim shops and businesses that were destroyed, some within 400 yards of then Colonel Blaskic's headquarters of the Kiseljak army barracks. She will testify about seeing the HVO forces in Kiseljak. She will describe them as being in absolute control of the city of Kiseljak and the surroundings. She will identify some of the types of weapons that they had at their disposal, including a tank. She will testify, Mr. President and your Honours, about personally meeting then Colonel Blaskic at what was described as his headquarters in the Kiseljak barracks. She will testify that she obtained a film permit from Colonel Blaskic. She will describe what effect that film permit had, in terms of her being able to do her business throughout the municipality on both of her visits. Lastly, Mr. President and your Honours, we will introduce into evidence the film. We will play the film, "We Are All Neighbours" and she will make observations about that film and describe certain parts of that film in greater detail. In respect of the indictment, Mr. President and your Honours, her testimony relates to the authority exercised by the accused, specifically paragraphs 3 and 4 of the indictment; it relates to persecution, paragraph 6.1; attacks on villages; and paragraph 6.3, destruction and plunder of property. Her testimony also relates to counts 2 to 4, unlawful attacks on civilians and civilian objects, and counts 11 through 13, the destruction and plunder of property. Lastly, it relates to count 14, the destruction of religious property. That concludes my summary, Mr. President and your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask you also to the intention of my colleagues. I would like to know approximately how much time you think your examination-in-chief will take?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: My examination-in-chief should take less than half an hour, Mr. President. The film is approximately 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have the intention of showing the whole film?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Without any further delay, will the Registry please then bring in the witness, Ms Deborah Christie. (Deborah Christie enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain -- we have a new usher here, so we have to make sure the usher takes on the good habits. Please have the witness remain standing. Madam, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am sorry to have you remain standing for a few moments. This is how the procedure is carried out here before this Tribunal. I would like to ask now, do you hear me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Would you please remind us of your last and first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Deborah Christie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing so that you may read the solemn declaration that the usher will put before you. MS DEBORAH CHRISTIE (Sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated. Madam, you have agreed to come and testify at the request of the Prosecutor before the International Criminal Tribunal in this case, in the matter of the Prosecution versus Colonel Blaskic, who is present in this courtroom. The Prosecutor has explained to you how this is going to proceed. I understand from the summary given by the Prosecution that you are a professional. The Prosecution has given us some background about you. The Prosecutor will guide you into areas which are of importance. There will be some introductory remarks or questions and then after that the Prosecutor will ask some questions. Please, you have the floor, Mr. Prosecutor. Examined by MR. HARMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Ms Christie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, please, tell us about your background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was trained as a journalist with the BBC and I then worked as a film-maker/journalist for Granada Television for six years working on their prime time news and current affairs programme which is called "World in Action". I came to work on a project, a strand called "Disappearing World" in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you currently do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am currently an Executive Producer at BBC Television. I am responsible for 25 staff who are making factual television programmes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a film-maker and as a journalist, have you won any awards and, if so, could you describe which awards you have won?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have won five awards; two of them specifically were for the Disappearing World programme in Bosnia. One of them was an international EMI award and the other one was the Royal Television Society in Britain's award.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms Christie, were you in the Kiseljak municipality and in the village of Visnjica from 22nd January 1993 to 14th February 1993, and then again from 29th April 1993 until 3rd May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there to make a film. I was working with an anthropologist called Tone Bringa who knew the area well. It was the first time I had been in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you give your answers, if you could give them in a narrative form. The court prefers that you give your testimony and I ask as few questions as possible. If you could tell us, please, about the background of the film, the genesis of the film, who Tone Bringa is, what she had done in the village before and what you then sought to achieve by making this particular film.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. The programme was made for a series called "Disappearing World". It is a series of television programmes which had been running for 10 years on Granada Television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Madam, I am going to ask you to speak a little more slowly for the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The film that I was making was for a strand on British television called "Disappearing World". This was a programme that had been running for 10 years. The style of the programme is to work with an anthropologist who has specialist knowledge in an area with a group of people and to try to make a film using the anthropologist's knowledge to reflect what is happening in that particular place or village. I was working with Tone Bringa, who is a Norwegian anthropologist. She had lived in the village of Visnjica for 15 months, five years previously; that is in 1988. She had studied the village. She was looking particularly, as an anthropologist, at the co-existence of different groups within the same village. The interest in the village was the co-existence primarily of Croat and Muslim. That was her specialist area. She knew the village very well, she had lived actually in the village for 15 months and when we returned to make the programme, Tone Bringa lived in the village of Visnjica for the dates described and the TV crew, camera and sound, lived in Kiseljak. I was living partly in Visnjica, partly in Kiseljak for that period of time. So, as well as making the film, I was actually living in the village and in Kiseljak. The film was an attempt to show what happened to civilians at a time of war; it was an attempt to document how peoples' lives changed, how their relationships with their communities and their families changed. It was made from an anthropological background, but it was designed to -- for an audience who we assumed would have no knowledge of Bosnia. The intention was to try to capture what was happening in peoples' lives and to hear those people talk candidly about what they were experiencing, what they were seeing and how their relationships with their family and their community were changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: In the course of making that film, you had ample opportunity to observe both the people in the village of Visnjica and the people in the village of Kiseljak. I am going to be asking you about those observations, and relate some of those observations to the Chamber, in just a minute. Once you started to make the film, did you have problems with the ability to move around and actually prepare that film? Could you describe those problems to the Trial Chamber and what you did to resolve those problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. We had already got accreditation from UNPROFOR, which is an ID card which we had reason to believe would enable us to work as journalists, as film-makers, in the area. In the first three or four days when we were in Visnjica and Kiseljak, on two or three occasions we were stopped by HVO soldiers who were inquiring what we were doing and why we were doing it and, on each occasion, required us to stop filming. On 29th January, we went with a Croat translator -- I went with a Croat translator to what I understood to be the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak, and we asked for permission from Colonel Blaskic, for a letter to make it clear what we were doing and to give us permission to operate in the area. We had been advised, both by UNPROFOR and by people within Kiseljak, that if we wished to move in the area, we must have some permission, particularly if we wanted to interview civilians. Bozica, who was the translator working with us on that day, we were taken into an office that I understood to be Colonel Blaskic's office. She went in, she spent some time in there. She came out with a piece of paper which was our permission. Colonel Blaskic came out, we shook hands, I took the piece of paper and I went. Over the next two and-a-half weeks, we used that piece of paper at least seven times --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we get into that, I am going to ask you that in just a minute. If I could ask for the assistance of the usher to place on the ELMO, Prosecutor's Exhibit 307. Mr. President, this is an enlargement of a previously admitted exhibit, Exhibit 75. I will ask that it be placed on the ELMO and I will going to ask the witness to identify it. (Handed). Now, Ms Christie, prior to coming to court, did I show you this photograph and did I ask you to circle the building where you met then Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you showed me that picture and I circled the office where I remember going in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That circle appears on the lower left-hand corner of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could again have the assistance of the usher? I would like to have Prosecutor's Exhibit 308 put on the ELMO. Mr. President, Exhibit 308 is a copy of the permit that was issued to Ms Christie and to Granada Television by Colonel Blaskic. Exhibit 308A is an English translation of that permit. I regret to say at this point I do not have a French translation of that and I will endeavour to get one. (Handed). Mr. Usher, if I could have the original language, not the English language version, but the Bosnian language version put on. Ms Christie on the ELMO is a permit. Do you recognise the document that is on the ELMO and can you tell the judges what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise the document. That was the document that we were given in Colonel Blaskic's office on 29th January. We were extremely grateful to him for that document and we used it many times over the next two weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me stay with a couple of other questions before we move on to the use of the permit. You say you went into an office that was described to you as the office of Colonel Blaskic. Can you describe the office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went in. There was a main waiting area with two soldiers. There was a room to the left, there was a room to the right. In the room to the right was where Bozica, who I was working with, went in to speak to Colonel Blaskic to get the permission. I waited where the guards were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, having secured what is Prosecutor's Exhibit 308, the permit, could you tell the judges what effect, and what force this particular document had in permitting you to conduct your business in the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were stopped on a regular basis, I would say two or three times a day, while we were filming, either at checkpoints or by HVO patrols in the village or in Kiseljak. On seven occasions that I wrote in my diary, we explained what we were doing, we showed the document and, on production of the document, we were then allowed to proceed. For example, I used the document three times on Saturday, 30th January: once in the village of Visnjica where we were stopped by an HVO patrol and I showed them the document and the gentleman who was looking at the document shouted to his colleague and said: "Blaskic, Blaskic", so we were allowed to proceed. Once in Kiseljak, when we were filming on the same day down by the market, and once on that same day when we were going towards Fojnica on the road at an official checkpoint. Perhaps most specifically, I used it the next Thursday, the 4th February, when we were stopped in the street in Kiseljak and we were asked to go with soldiers to see Josip Boro who we were introduced to as the President of the Opstina in Kiseljak. He wished to ask us questions about what we were doing and why we were there. I showed him the letter from Colonel Blaskic and, after some discussion, he went away. He showed it to someone, he came back. He was content, having seen the letter, that it was okay for us to proceed. We were, at the time, trying to make an arrangement to film in a factory. He said he would try to facilitate us filming in the factory. On Monday, 8th February, the cameraman and I were again stopped in Kiseljak and asked to accompany the soldiers, first to what was known as the police station in the main street in Kiseljak. Then we were taken on to the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak. We were detained for about an hour and-a-half in the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak. Again, a lot of questions about what we were doing. Again, we showed the piece of paper. On that occasion they particularly wanted the original, not just a photocopy -- we had photocopied it. We gave them the original. They took it away; they came back and they were satisfied by the piece of paper that we were in order, we could proceed about our business and it was fine for them to film. We used it at checkpoints where there was an HVO checkpoint crossing the road. Sometimes you would be waved through a checkpoint, sometimes you would be stopped. I can remember occasions when we were stopped. Everything in our van was taken out, everything was searched. There was a definite sense that they did not wish us to proceed. Then we showed them the letter and they were satisfied with that. They went on to continue their search, but the tone was very different after we had shown the letter. So, for example, on that occasion, they started to search our picnic box, but after they had seen the letter they made a joke of it and said it was funny that we had a picnic box. The effect of that letter -- which we were grateful for -- was that it enabled us to film, it enabled us to go about our business. It was a letter that a variety of soldiers on different checkpoints seemed to understand. On several occasions, although I do not speak Serbo-Croat myself, I heard reference to Blaskic as something being shouted to their colleagues as an acknowledgement of what the piece of paper was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also use the same permit when you returned to Visnjica and Kiseljak on 29th April and use it through 3rd May 1993, and did it have the same effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I used it on two occasions. Once in the village of Visnjica. It was, by that time, extremely difficult to get into the village. There was an HVO checkpoint at the entrance to the village and we went in with the Canadian Battalion convoy. We were driving at the back of the convoy. As we drove into the village after the mosque, we were stopped -- the convoy proceeded, we were stopped and asked what we were doing. Again we showed the Blaskic letter and we were told that we could stay for an hour to do what we needed to do, but the letter, again, was significant. The second time in the April/May period was we were stopped coming back from Fojnica on the road between Fojnica and Kiseljak. Again, we showed the paper and we were allowed through the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Ms Christie, I would like to focus your attention on the village of Visnjica. I would, first of all, as you to just make your general observations to the judges. What was the village of Visnjica like between January 22nd and February 14th of 1993? Could you just give us some general impressions and views?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a small village in which everybody knew everybody else, although there were obvious changes caused by the war. For example, the men who would normally be working in Sarajevo were in the village rather than working. People were attempting to get about their normal lives. They were looking after animals, they were chopping wood, they were occasionally going to Kiseljak to the market to buy things or sell things. There was a level of tension, but Muslim and Croat were still going in and out of each other's houses, they were taking tea, they were taking coffee. While they were anxious about the war at that time in the village, there was a sense that they would get on with their ordinary lives. There were things to be done, they had to manage their animals, they had to look after their houses and gardens. As I say, when we first arrived the Croats and Muslims were still visiting each other's houses. That changed in the three weeks we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were there on your initial trip, did you see any HVO military patrols come through the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw patrols that would be two soldiers on foot, armed, patrolling the village on three or four occasions. They would walk up through the village, up the hill, round and down again, those were day-time patrols. We saw three in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the judges the presence of Bosnian military soldiers, military depots, communication centres? Were there any military targets of any kind in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw any Bosnian Army presence in the village of any type. We were aware that some of the Bosnian Muslim men had their own guns, which they had had as reservists in Tito's army. When we were there, the Bosnian Muslim men were still going about once every 10 days up to Sarajevo to fight on the front at Sarajevo with their own guns, that was the most I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were making your film, you were in and out of Muslim homes in the village at various times unannounced and announced and the like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, at any time -- any time while you were in the village -- see anything that resembled a military presence of the Bosnian Army, aside from these few soldiers who would go to the front-line and back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved very freely in the village and we were welcomed in everybody's house, even unannounced, for the whole period we were there. We would sometimes simply knock on peoples' doors. No, I did not see any presence of Bosnian Army. I was aware of five Muslim men who went up to the Sarajevo front. I was also aware of the presence of a patrol, which, in the week prior to us being there, had been a joint Muslim Croat patrol around the village. In the week we arrived, that had changed and it was no longer a joint patrol. For a period of about 10 days, the Bosnian Muslim men decided to conduct their own patrol within the village. This amounted to six men who would gather in a house and two at a time they would walk around the village at night, between about 10.00 and 1.00 in the morning to patrol their own houses. By the third week we were there, that patrol had finished because the HVO had put a curfew in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did each of those Muslims who participated in the patrol -- you said there were six -- did each of them have a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I remember on the evening we spent with them there was some discussion because, between the six of them, they only had five guns and also the evening that we were there, they asked to borrow our torch because, between them, they did not have a torch, so they were extremely ill-equipped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, focusing your attention on your first visit to the Kiseljak/Visnjica area, I would like to focus your attention on Kiseljak. Could you tell the judges your observations of Kiseljak before the attacks in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. Kiseljak was still functioning very well as a large village, a small town. Most of the shops were still opened when we arrived, they were still trading. There was quite a strong HVO presence. I would say that any time when you were standing in the street, if you waited in the street for five or 10 minutes you would see an HVO patrol of some kind in Kiseljak, but it was still definitely functioning. People were going about their business. The market was running two, sometimes three days a week. The shops were open. There was a factory in Kiseljak which was running the whole time that we were there. Over the period of the three weeks we were there, the situation became much more tense in Kiseljak. On two or three occasions we saw the HVO clear the streets, perhaps at 3.00 in the afternoon they would come with a convoy on one occasion led by a tank. On other occasions it would simply be jeeps with Croatian flags and soldiers. They would clear the streets, they would instruct everybody to get off the streets for a period of time. They would clear the streets for maybe one or two hours. Then life would resume and the shops would open up again. But there was a clear sense that the HVO were in command of that town, that village. We used the shops to buy our own food in Kiseljak, so we were regular visitors to the shops in Kiseljak. We noticed that on -- around the 2nd February, it appeared that all the Muslim shops were closed, we were unclear why that was, but we believed that it was possibly because they had been stopped at checkpoints and had not been allowed to come in to open their own shops. We did not know but our observation was that around the 2nd the Muslim shops were closed. Some of the Muslim shops were open again on the 3rd. On the morning of the 5th we went into Kiseljak and we observed that at least eight of the Muslim shops had been smashed and vandalised. We did not see any Croat shops that were in any way destroyed or damaged and the shops were very well-known to Tone Bringa, who knew the area very well, so she could identify very clearly which ones were Muslim and it seemed very clear that the Muslim ones had been targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of specific questions about points that you mentioned: did you ever see in Kiseljak any Bosnian Army soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described the tank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of markings did the tank have on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tank had red and white chequered Croatian colouring on the side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also described at least eight Muslim shops that had been destroyed in the village of Kiseljak. Approximately what was the distance between those shops that had been destroyed and Colonel Blaskic's headquarters at the Kiseljak army barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were spread throughout the town between half a mile -- half a kilometre and a kilometre from the HVO headquarters, the shops that were damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to your visit of 29th April to 3rd May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, first of all, why you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had been in telephone contact with UNPROFOR in Kiseljak, which was our only way of getting any knowledge about what had happened in the area, and we understood -- we phoned on either the 21st or 22nd April and we were told by UNPROFOR that there had been a lot of fighting and military activity in the Visnjica area. So, we made the decision to return to see what had happened and to complete the film. We travelled up through Mostar to Kiseljak. When we arrived at Visnjica, the village was completely sealed off by HVO checkpoints and we were uncertain what the situation was. So, we went back to UNPROFOR and we went back into Visnjica two days later, accompanied by Canadian battalion. On that -- by now you will appreciate we knew the village quite well, but also Tona Bringa knew the village very intimately; she had been there for 15 months. So, we drove in on the back of a Canadian battalion convoy. It became clear, as we went up the main street in Visnjica, that all the Muslim houses had been destroyed. On some occasions, there would be a Croat house, then a Muslim house then a Croat house and the Muslim one in the middle would be destroyed, severely damaged and on several occasions burned out. The mosque was also severely damaged. Many of the houses where we had filmed with Muslim families were completely destroyed. It was clear from the state of the houses, which we knew quite well by then, that the people had had to leave in a terrible hurry, that they had taken absolutely nothing. There was, right the way through the village, evidence of Muslim houses being destroyed. I should add here, just as a detail, we were stopped on that occasion in the village and we once again showed the pass. I mentioned that before. When we were in the village, we were in the village only for about an hour. We saw, I would say, a maximum of 10 Bosnian Muslim people. That includes one elderly woman who we knew to be senile, her family had not persuaded her to leave. That included some refugees who had come to Visnjica as refugees and had not moved on, but a maximum of 10, I would say, Bosnian Muslim people in the village. We stopped to speak to Slavka, as you will see in the film. This was a Croat woman who we got to know very well and we had been into her house many times. We asked her what had happened and she explained that the Muslim houses had been burned. She also explained that she had been -- that the Croats had been warned in advance that this was going to happen, so she and her family had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she explain to you who burned the Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She told us the Croat soldiers had burned the Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that there had been systematic destruction in targeting of Muslim houses and outbuildings, such as barns, in the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was very clear it was not random. One of the interesting things about Visnjica is that the houses are completely intermingled, Croat house, Muslim house, Croat house, Muslim house. There was very clear targeting of Muslim houses which had been destroyed and Croat houses that had been left standing. In the same road there would be Muslim houses destroyed and Croat houses left standing. We asked Slavka if any of the Croat houses had been damaged and she said she thought that two barns had been damaged but no Croat houses had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in a few minutes we are going to play the film "We Are All Neighbours", the film that you prepared. I would be very interested in your, very quickly, summarising for the judges the film. Then I am going to ask you about a couple of the points on the film in advance so the judges and counsel can be alert to particular parts of the film. Could you give us first a brief summary of the film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The film is 50 minutes. It is -- as I said before, it comes from an anthropological perspective. It is an attempt to hear the people of the village talk about what they are seeing, what they are experiencing. What we witnessed over the period of the first three and-a-half weeks that we were there was the progression from a village where people were still neighbours, were still going in and out of each others houses. Three and-a-half weeks later on, that had completely broken down. The HVO patrols were regular within the village. There was a belief that the HVO had built a gun implement above the village. So the first 40 minutes of the film charts that three weeks in the life of the village when relationships in the village broke down. We then went back to Britain and what you see in the last eight minutes of the film was when we returned. When we returned, we filmed, as I say, just for one hour in the village itself and we also interviewed some of the Muslims who had fled from the village who were now in Visoko and in other areas outside of Kiseljak. So, what you hear in the last eight minutes is their account of what happened in the three days when, as they describe it, the village was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when the film is played, feel free to make comments as the film is shown. I want to direct your attention to a few particular points. The film, itself, shows the few Muslim villagers who went on these patrols, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also shows a Bosniak by the name of Nurija who was the principal Muslim in the film. It shows him walking with about four or five other men, armed, walking up a hill, then returning from a hill. Where was that particular part of the film shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was shot outside Sarajevo. We filmed the men going out of the village. They then, in fact, went in a bus, which we did not film, and we picked them up at the front-line in Sarajevo where they were at that time part of the Sarajevo Defence against the Serb offensive. So that is the context in which their visit to the front-line was at that time, about once every 10 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if, during the showing of the film, you could inform us when these shots are at the front-lines positions in Sarajevo and in the village of Visnjica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Second of all, I would like to draw your attention to a part of the film where there is a Bosniak man with a walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that part of the film?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges now who that man was, if you know him by name or by ethnicity, and what happened to the walkie-talkie and when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That man was a Bosnian Muslim who went to the front-line every 10 days. We film him in somebody's sitting room talking on a walkie-talkie. On 30th January, he was detained for about four or five hours and his walkie-talkie was taken from him. As I understand it, in the next two and-a-half weeks that we were there certainly, he no longer had a walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who took the walkie-talkie from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO took the walkie-talkie from him. He was detained on the 30th for four hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Lastly, there is a portion on the film where the sister of a woman named Slavka appears on the film. She is very upset and she describes events where Muslims attacked her village and the surrounding area. Can you tell us what happened to that woman and what happened to her home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. Slavka's sister, who is a woman you will see in red in the film, arrived in some distress at Slavka's house. She had heard they were going to attack her village, her village was about 12 miles away. She had heard that they were going to attack the village and she had fled and come to stay with her sister, Slavka. Psychologically, this was an important moment for Slavka because it was a moment when she suddenly became extremely frightened. We went back to Slavka's house two days later and we understood that, in fact, her sister had gone back to her own house; that the rumour that there was going to be an attack had been unfounded and her house was okay. She was particularly anxious about the freezer. She was worried that the freezer would be spoilt. That is why I remember it so well. She had gone back to her house and her house had not, in fact, been damaged. Slavka confirmed that to us because when Slavka herself fled from Visnjica she went to stay with her sister whose house was still intact. There is a point in the film where the impression is that Slavka's sister's house had been destroyed but, in fact, we discovered that her house had not been destroyed and Slavka went to stay there later. There is one other point I should perhaps make, at the very end of the film, there is a shot of a dead horse and that is the only shot that is not shot in Visnjica. It was shot in a different village on the UN patrol that we were with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it shot in the area of Gomionica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Feel free, in the course of the film, to make comments and point out these areas and other areas you think are relevant about the film. If we could have the lights dimmed, please and if we could play "We Are All Neighbours".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. (3.20 pm) (Film played to court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the right is the Bosnian army volunteer. (Film continued) That is the walkie-talkie radio I was talking about, which was confiscated two days later by the HVO. This is at Sarajevo, on the front in Sarajevo. (Film continued) Again, all of this sequence is just outside Sarajevo. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Still outside Sarajevo. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is back at Sarajevo on the front-line. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Back at Sarajevo on the front-line. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is coming back down from the front-line in Sarajevo, then got on a bus and drove back to the village. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This woman had arrived from Rogatica. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is near Visoko, outside the village. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the woman I was referring to who returned to her house two days later and it was still intact. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was our second visit. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is in Visoko. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the Canadian battalion. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the only shot that is not in Visnjica, with the horse. (Film continued)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These pictures are contrasting what it was like in January to what it was like in May. (Film continued) (4.17 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are we going to take a recess, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. If I could move for the admission of the exhibits, which would be 307, 308 and the film, then I have concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We are now going to take a 30-minute recess, so the interpreters will have an opportunity to rest. We will reconvene at quarter to the hour. (4.17 pm) (A short break) (4.54 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is now in session. Please bring in Colonel Blaskic. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The interpreters, I hope, are well rested. Very well. The Prosecution has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have concluded my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Ms Christie, you will now then be questioned in cross-examination, which will be led by Mr. Hayman, who is the Defence counsel for the accused. Cross-examined by MR. HAYMAN

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms Christie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the anthropologist, Ms Bringa, lived in the village of Visnjica in 1988, do you know whether she lived with a particular family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She lived, as I understand it, with two or three different families, but I do not know which ones she lived with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you and she were residing, at least in part, during your visits to Visnjica in 1993, did you reside with one or more particular families?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we lived -- when we were in Kiseljak, we lived with the Komsic family, a Croatian family in Kiseljak. When we were in Visnjica we lived with Nusreta and Nurija, who you see in the film, so we were divided between a Croat and Muslim family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Miss Bringa, in 1988, lived with the characters Nusreta and Nurija during part of her stay in Visnjica in that year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly in part of her stay, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about Exhibit 308.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that is still on the ELMO which is fine. We can keep it there. I would like to ask you about the occasion on which you obtained this permit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go in the office that you have said was represented to you to be Colonel Blaskic's office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went with Bozica Komsic, who was translating for us, into a building where we were told, "this is Colonel Blaskic's office". I waited. She went through to an extra room to discuss with Colonel Blaskic. I did not go into the extra room. I stayed in the outside room. Then Colonel Blaskic came out with the piece of paper and we shook hands in the outside room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may pause for a moment after your answer to allow the interpreters to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Similarly, if you could pause after my question, it would be helpful to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you enter any office in this complex or compound that bore signs or indica of a personal office, such as pictures of family, or the like, relating to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go into the inner office which was described as Colonel Blaskic's office. No, I did not go in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any markings on any of the doors or buildings that indicated either that this was the headquarters of the operational zone for Central Bosnia, or that any particular office was the office of Colonel Tihomir Blaskic? Did you ever see any markings of either of that sort?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember any markings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason that I believed it was Colonel Blaskic's office was that we were working with Bozica Komsic, who was a resident of Kiseljak, who was also attached as translator to UNPROFOR, and she described to me that we would go to Colonel Blaskic's office to see if we could explain the situation and get a permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ms Christie, when you respond, if you could turn towards the judges when giving your answer, as much as possible. I know you are also trying to follow the questions put to you by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Was Colonel Blaskic helpful in giving you this permit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was very helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, to read the printed matter in the seal on Exhibit 308, which has not been translated in the translation. Could you read the seal for the record, Mr. Nobilo, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the upper corner is: "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna", and in the bottom part of the seal, after "1", it says: "Kiseljak (...Spoke in Bosnian...) and the Defence Department."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: You have heard from the translation of this seal that this is not the seal of the headquarters of the operational zone, Central Bosnia, it is the seal of a local brigade headquarters, the Ban Jelacic Brigade, which was based in Kiseljak, BiH. Did anyone represent to you at any time that the building you were in was anything other than the command of the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, other than what you have already described?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would object. She has testified what the office was represented to her as being; that is the office of Colonel Blaskic. She never said that it was represented to her as being the office of the Ban Jelacic Brigade, so I would object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I sustain that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Then tell us, Ms Christie, why, if you were at Colonel Blaskic's headquarters, why do you not think he would have a seal from his own headquarters with which to put a stamp on the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I do not agree with this line of questioning. The witness told you very exactly what she did and what she wanted to do. I think for this witness to be able to do her work she knew what she had to go and where she had to go to obtain what she needed to get. She felt she was at the office of Colonel Blaskic. I do not think you should continue with this line of questioning. Please go on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Were you told how long Colonel Blaskic had been in Kiseljak when you saw him on 29th January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn any information about how long thereafter he remained in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding from UNPROFOR was, prior to 29th January, that we would have to go to this office where we would find Colonel Blaskic in order to get permission. Once we had the piece of paper, I would have to say honestly I had very little further interest in that area. We were filming and, as far as I was concerned, I needed to know that this piece of paper would still work for me as a working document which it did on every occasion we tried to use it. As far as -- my concern was that the paper with Blaskic's signature continued to work for me. I had no further knowledge about Mr. Blaskic's movements. I asked no further questions about it either. It was not of particular interest to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that true, that you had no knowledge of Colonel Blaskic's whereabouts when you returned to the area and stayed between the 29th April and 3rd May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no further knowledge of where Colonel Blaskic was. I had no need to know where Colonel Blaskic was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am moving to a new area. I simply want to note that the Defence notes its objection that Exhibit 308 was not produced to us before today. It was discoverable under Rule 68 because it directly impeaches a witness that testified on February 24th, 1993, before your Honours in closed session, as to the whereabouts of Colonel Blaskic, vis-à-vis the conflict going on at that time in the Busovaca municipality. It is also a statement of the accused within the meaning of this court's order of January 27, 1997, interpreting Rule 66A. We will file a brief on this subject next week. I am not seeking a ruling from the court; I am not seeking a response from the Prosecutor. I am simply noting our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, I think we have a memory of it. Your note has been entered into the transcripts. Please try to be as brief as possible. If you wish to file a brief, then I must say that we are not going to spend our entire trial trying to resolve issues which are very important (sic), so I hope that you will be able to meet with the Prosecutor and then we will deal with this later on from reading the transcript. Does the Prosecutor have any objections at all with regard to the remarks made by Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: They have been addressed previously, Mr. President, in respect of whether an order constitutes a statement. I have no further remarks, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Then that particular debate is closed. Please go on with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Ms Christie, the village of Visnjica, is it fair to say the village is elongated and stretches along a road which goes to the south-west from Polje-Visnjica, which is on the main Kiseljak-Busovaca road; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the village was roughly two-thirds Muslim, one-third Croat; correct? Can you give us a general idea of the size of the village; 100 people, 200 people, 300 people, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly from memory and it would be difficult at that time to put an exact figure because the village was, at times, swollen by refugees arriving, and at times evacuated almost by people going away. I would say around 600-700 people, maybe a little more, but I would have to check that for accuracy. As I say, it was a village influxed with refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is your best estimate as to the total population? If you could respond audibly so there is an answer on the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the two ethnic groups -- Croats and Muslims within the village -- were they interspersed or was one group collected in one area and the other group collected, say, at the other end of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interspersed throughout the village. So, on the main road, from the road up to the mosque, there were interspersed Croat and Muslim houses. On the right flank of the village, which was the newer side of the village as you went up to the mosque, again, there were interspersed Croat and Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the narrator in the film or did someone else narrate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us, as narrator of the film, at one juncture, I believe, that the character Nurija, together with his immediate neighbours, formed a patrol to patrol their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that patrol consisted of roughly five or six men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They had between them five or six weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some of which were depicted in the film; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you agree: they patrolled an immediate area consisting roughly of their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go out on patrol with them, so I could not tell you exactly where they patrolled. My understanding was that they walked around their homes in the village, but I never went actually on patrol with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss with anyone the presence of other Muslim patrols in other parts of the village where Muslims resided?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not ask and you were not told whether that existed; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask and I was not told, although I should make it clear that of the six men you see, to my knowledge, two of them live in the older part of the village and three of them live in the newer part of the village. Of the six that I saw, they came from slightly different parts of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss with anyone how many members of the BiH Territorial Defence resided in Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that again that you did not ask, or it never came up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not asked and it never came up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point there was a curfew which impaired with the activity of these patrols. Were you told what the terms of this curfew were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were specifically affected by the curfew because we were specifically told by the HVO in Kiseljak, when they stopped us once at 7.00 in the evening, that there was now a curfew from 8.00 and nobody must go out after 8.00. That was my first knowledge of the curfew. We heard of the curfew from a number of different people in the village, Croat and Muslim, and our understanding of the curfew -- which was sometimes at 8.00, sometimes at 10.00 -- was that no-one should venture out after that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described a visit to Kiseljak, I believe, on 8th February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you saw what you believed to be certain shops that had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 5th February was when we saw the shops that had been damaged. The 5th, Friday 5th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Did you investigate yourself and speak to shopkeepers to determine whose shops those were or were you told in general terms: "These are Muslim shops", by someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We asked -- you will remember that Tone Bringa knew Kiseljak very well, so she knew most of the shopkeepers. We asked Slavka, who is Croat, and Tone and Sabina and Sakreta who you see in the film walking past the shops. We were told by all of those three people that the shops were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to determine who had damaged or vandalised those shops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you returned to the village of Visnjica. Are you able to tell us the date on which you returned? I understand you went back between 29th April and 3rd May. Are you able to be more specific with respect to the date you returned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am pretty certain we actually got into the village on 1st May with the Canadian battalion, but I do not have a specific note of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you determine out of the houses that had housed the 600 or 700 people living in the village, how many of the houses were burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you an exact count of how many of the houses were burned. We filmed all of the houses which we knew had featured prominently in the film that were burned and we were aware, as we went through the main road, which is the old village, that there was a very consistent pattern of, in the older part of the village, all of the Muslim houses had been destroyed or burned. I could not give you a count for the whole village, no. You will appreciate we were only allowed in for an hour so we had to prioritise what we were going to film.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of that hour did you drive the length of Visnjica, given that Visnjica stretches out along the length of a road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we went right the way round the length of the road. We then went up to the right, as you are looking at the mosque, where there is the newer part of the village and we went through -- there is a network of roads there. We went all the way through all of those networks. It is a pattern of the UNPROFOR, what they call "routine patrols", that they attempt to go down each road within a village so we went down every road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to give us a proportion of the total number of dwellings that appeared to have been burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not want to speculate on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one juncture in the film, as narrator, you said that the fighting was coming closer and that now it was Croats and Muslims fighting; do you recall that juncture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was? When was it that that fighting was audible from Visnjica? I am directing your attention back to the first visit in January/February 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be between 1st February and 8th February. You will appreciate that the manner in which we were collecting information at this stage is that we would hear what people were telling us. We would then do our best to check with UNPROFOR in Kiseljak what exactly was happening. So, I could not be more specific than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from your interviews what had happened -- strike that. Were the sounds of fighting coming from the north-west, that is towards Busovaca, Kacuni, Bilalovac, from those locations towards Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in the village told us that that is where the noise of the fighting was coming from. I am not a military expert, so I would not be able to tell you with any precision what the noise of the fighting was, which was why we only put things in the film which we actually clarified with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn from your interviews what had occurred in the course of that fighting in the direction of Kacuni/Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that fighting have an impact on the emotions and mental state on the inhabitants of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Every time the fighting came nearer, the tension got higher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the uncertainty and, in a sense, the competition, represented by the negotiations of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, did that add to the tension in the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me to make a generalisation about the mood of the village of Visnjica which I would be wary of. What we said in the film very specifically was that people were certainly watching the television every night to learn the latest developments in the Vance-Owen negotiations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You showed an image of an individual in a uniform speaking over a walkie-talkie in the residents, I take it, of someone in Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn who that individual was talking to on the radio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We saw in the film a description by a refugee from -- I believe it was Rogatica -- of events there. Is it your understanding that Rogatica was a location that was attacked by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding. The sequence is there in the film to show the movement of refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nusreta says at one point in the film that Nurija would rather fight than give up his gun; do you recall that passage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to Nurija and confirm that, first of all, that was also his sentiment? This is, again, during your first visit, that was his mental state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your second visit, did you confirm that, in fact, he had done that; he had fought and attempted to defend his location in the conflict that began, I take it, on Easter Sunday, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know specifically what he did. What he told us in the interview was that they attempted to defend themselves over the three-day period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that battle or fight lasted for three days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The description of the events of the three days from Nurija and Nusreta was that on the Sunday morning, most of the Croatian civilians left. On the Sunday there was fighting, and by Sunday evening, most of the Bosnian men had left and Monday and Tuesday was when the houses were burned. There were still civilians in the houses when they were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you said in the film that Nusreta and Nurija left after five days of violence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Nusreta left after five days of violence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Nurija then left after three days --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were separate at that time. Nurija -- I am not sure when Nurija left, my understanding was that he left on the Monday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you been given any additional information concerning how many Muslim fighters or Croat fighters took place in the battle you are describing on Sunday, Monday, Tuesday and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, let me be clear that my understanding from the people we spoke to was that the fighting, the crossfire was on Sunday and on Monday the houses were burned. You appreciate that we were not in the area at the time, we returned 10 days later, so we were going on only the witnesses we spoke to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With respect to the persons that were killed in that conflict, did all of the information you obtained, with respect to specific perpetrators of those killings, were all the perpetrators neighbours of the deceased persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the film there are several passages to that effect; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other information did you obtain in the course of speaking with residents of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specifically in the witnesses that we spoke to; there are five or six people within the village who they identify, who were involved in the fighting. They then refer, on Monday, to outsiders coming in, in HVO uniform. That is confirmed by Slavka, the Croat who we interviewed in the village, who told us that it was what she calls "foreigners", then she calls "outsiders", by that I mean they were Croats, but not Croats from the village. That is her description of who was involved in the fighting on the Monday and Tuesday. That tallies with what the Muslim witnesses also told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the fighting on Sunday, April 18th, 1993, insofar as you were able to determine, was between neighbours; that is local inhabitants of the village of Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And outsiders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And outsiders as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you and what did the persons tell you about outsiders participating in fighting in Visnjica on Sunday, April 18th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slavka, who is Croat, told us that the soldiers arrived on Sunday morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you referring now to the statement she makes on the film or some additional statement she made to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We discussed with her in -- for about 10 or 15 minutes and that is what she told us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned in April, you said , as narrator, that the village had been sealed off by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the purpose of that sealing off? Was it to prevent looting or for some other purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the purpose. I know only that when we drove up to Visnjica on 29th April, we drove up to the turning off the main road into Visnjica. There was an area checkpoint and when we drove close to it they picked their guns up from the floor and armed themselves. We had been advised by UNPROFOR that they believed that the village was sealed off by the HVO and they would advise us not to go in. On the basis of the UNPROFOR advice and the checkpoint we did not go in, but I have no knowledge why it was sealed off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described seeing a tank in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any pictures of the tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you date your sighting of the tank? Do you have notes or a log or diary or is it your recollection you are relying on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am relying entirely on my recollection. When we stayed in Kiseljak we stayed with a Croat family on the main road in Kiseljak, and this particular sighting we were actually just washing and preparing food in the place where we were staying. We saw out of the window on to the main road. I did not make a note of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay in Kiseljak during all the portion of your second visit in April/May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The scenes from the front near Sarajevo where there is a picture of uniformed men going down into a bunker, if you will; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the location of that portion of the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you an exact location of that, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the scene in the film when Nusreta picks up a plate that was three portions of a dessert and says in substance; Croatia, Bosnia, Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you come to understand that what she meant by that was, first, Croatia, that is portions of the Kiseljak municipality; then portions of the Kiseljak municipality in and around Bilalovac as being part of Bosnia; then the other half of the middle portion, those portions of the Busovaca municipality in and around Kacuni; then finally Croatia being Busovaca -- the remainder of the Busovaca municipality; did you gain that understanding from that incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I should give you a little more context from it. This was a social evening. The women was singing and joking. This was not an attempt to give us a military briefing on the situation. This was something by way of a more light-hearted comment which expressed their views. If you listen, I think there is a voice of another woman saying: "So Bosnia will only be 18 inches wide". It was not in any sense an attempt to give us a military briefing, it was an attempt to try to describe the psychology of how they felt at the time in the context of an evening with a lot of women who were singing and talking and conversing. It certainly was not an attempt on Nusreta's part to draw a specific military map for it. It was more to give us a sense of their emotion at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms Christie. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMAN
utterances.text: I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms Christie.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you started your enterprise, you mentioned that you had permission of the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And this permission did not serve you much, so you went and obtained the permission signed by Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It is his signature from his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I can see the signature in the -- at least on Serbo-Croat paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This permission opened the doors for you? You said that you were stopped on seven occasions by checkpoints, police stations, and when they saw the permission, they shouted to each other: "Blaskic, Blaskic", and they submitted to the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the seven very specific occasions I documented in the period of two and-a-half weeks, they would stop us; there would be an atmosphere of some military authority. I would not say hostility, but military authority. They would attempt to block our way. We would show them the piece of paper. On every occasion that would change the mood and they would agree to let us go on our way. On three occasions they specifically talked amongst other: "Blaskic, Blaskic", and there was a very clear sense that if we had this piece of paper it was okay. They would let us past, they would let us continue our filming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did they not mention any other name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No-one challenged the order openly or implicitly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody challenged the order. When we went to see Josip Boro, who was introduced to us as the President of the Opstina in Kiseljak, he asked us questions about what we were doing in Kiseljak. We then showed him the order. He was then very happy with what we were doing. He took the order into another room to show it to somebody else and he came back, and that further clarification seemed to make him completely comfortable that we could then proceed. As I say, after we had shown him the order, he tried to help us a little with our filming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So, the order had its effect on everybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that this lady, Slavka, declared that she was speaking, saying that the Muslim houses are burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And these houses were clearly targeted, I use your words. Did she say by whom they were clearly targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She said that soldiers came from the outside. By that I mean they were Croatian soldiers, but they were from the outside, is what she said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were they HVO or from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She did not specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: "Outside", does that mean Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My understanding was when she said "outside", she meant outside the village. That was my understanding at the time. She did not specify whether they were HV or HVO. She did not specify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: She said that they had been informed beforehand about what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By the soldiers too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was informed -- her own son was in the HVO, and the way that she described it to us, the HVO had come to the village and warned the Croat villagers to flee, to leave, at 4.30 in the morning; 8.00, the fighting started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the Croats also left the village or did they stay and feel safe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of the Croat women and children left the village. When we returned -- as I understand it at the time of the meeting, when we were there, which was 10 or 11 days after the fighting, it seemed to us that the Croats were back in the village. By that I mean all the Croats we knew were in their houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And their houses were intact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their houses were completely intact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You said the village was two-thirds Muslims. What was the population, approximately? I am not asking difficult questions, if you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am guessing around 700, but I have to say specifically here that the population was in flux because people would go -- peoples' relatives would arrive from somewhere and they would expand and then go again. I do not know precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Whatever the number was, you said only 10 remained, 10 were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only saw 10. I cannot tell you how many remained because I was only in the village for one hour. I could not go into every house. When I was there, in the hour I was there, I saw a maximum of 10 Muslims. That included one woman who is in the film, who we understand has a little dementia, and her family made her come away but she had not, and some of the people who were themselves refugees, so were not inhabitants of the village but had been lives there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The rest of the people, were they residents of the village or Croats coming from other places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people -- the Croats who we saw in the village were residents of the village. The ones that we knew. They were in the houses going about their business, looking after their garden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In the film I think there was an old woman crying and she said: 20 men were butchered and everything was destroyed, while she was crying. Her daughter was killed, her niece was killed, but she did not say by whom. Did you understand -- perhaps I missed that. Were they in the Serbian front or were they in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is about halfway through the film, not at the end of the film, a woman in purple?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She came from Rogatica. My understanding was that that was Serb action against her family. But the reason she is filmed in our film is because she was demonstrating that refugees were coming into the village from different areas.
